title: How did early humans learn, create, and move?
essentialQuestion: How did shared knowledge help humans adapt in different places?
learningGoal: Use clues that archaeologists find to explain how shared knowledge helped early humans adapt to new places.

warmUp.question: What is one skill that people usually learn from someone else?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.

cards.title: Four clues from early human sites

cases.name: Clue 1
cases.body: A stone cutting tool with many small marks along one edge.

cases.name: Clue 2
cases.body: A hearth (a fireplace) with layers of ash and burned seeds.

cases.name: Clue 3
cases.body: Handprints and pictures of animals on a rock wall.

cases.name: Clue 4
cases.body: Tools with the same shape, found at sites far apart.

sections.heading: People pass knowledge on
sections.text: Many animals can learn, and some even use simple tools. But humans are especially good at sharing what they learn, because we use language to explain ideas in detail. A child can learn a skill from an older person, improve it and then teach it to others. In this way, knowledge can grow from one generation to the next. Some historians call this collective learning. For example, one person might find a better way to shape a stone tool. Others copy the idea, change it a little and pass it on, so it is not lost when one person stops using it.
sections.simpler: Many animals learn. Some even use tools. But humans are very good at sharing what they learn. We use words to explain ideas. A child learns a skill from an older person. Then the child makes it better. Later, the child teaches others. So knowledge grows from one generation to the next. This is called collective learning. A good idea does not end with one person.

sections.heading: Clues from early human sites
sections.text: Early humans did not leave any written records, so how do we know about them? An archaeologist studies the things that people left behind, such as tools, bones, footprints, fireplaces and art. A worn tool can show how people used it. Burned seeds in a hearth can show what people cooked. Art shows that people used signs and symbols. In Blombos Cave in South Africa, someone cut a neat pattern into a piece of red rock about 75,000 years ago. However, one object rarely proves a whole story, so archaeologists compare many finds from different places and times.
sections.simpler: Early humans did not write. So how do we learn about them? An archaeologist studies things that people left behind. Tools, bones and art are all clues. A worn tool shows how people used it. Burned seeds in a hearth show what people cooked. In South Africa, people marked a red rock with lines. That was about 75,000 years ago. But one object does not tell the whole story. So archaeologists look at many finds.

sections.heading: Moving and adapting to new places
sections.text: Scientists explain that our species first lived in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Over many thousands of years, groups slowly spread into Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas. This did not happen in one long trip. It happened a little at a time, over many generations. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and seasons, and they made new tools and clothes. To reach Australia, people had to cross the sea, so they must have built boats. A tool may look simple, but making it took planning, skill and teaching.
sections.simpler: Scientists say our kind of human first lived in Africa. That was about 300,000 years ago. Slowly, groups spread to other parts of the world. This took many thousands of years. It did not happen in one trip. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and weather. To reach Australia, they crossed the sea in boats. A tool may look simple. But making it took skill and teaching.

glossary.definition: Knowledge that people share, improve and pass on over time.
glossary.example: Teaching others a better way to make a stone tool is collective learning.

glossary.definition: All the people born around the same time.
glossary.example: Grandparents and grandchildren belong to different generations.

glossary.definition: A person who studies the past by looking at things people left.
glossary.example: An archaeologist might study a stone tool to learn how people lived.

glossary.definition: A place on the ground where people make a fire.
glossary.example: The hearth had layers of ash, so people used it many times.

glossary.definition: To change so you can live well in a new situation.
glossary.example: Early humans adapted to cold places by making warm clothes.

write.prompt: Use two of the four clues to explain how early humans may have learned from each other. Include one thing the clues cannot tell us.
sentenceStarters: The clues suggest that early humans ...
But the clues cannot tell us ...
selfCheck: I used two of the clues.
I explained how people may have learned from each other.
I named one thing the clues cannot tell us.
write.example: The clues suggest that early humans learned skills from each other. Clue 4 shows tools with the same shape at sites far apart. This may mean that people copied a good design and taught it to others. Another clue is the hearth with layers of ash. People may have used the same fireplace many times and shared what they knew about fire and food. Together, these clues suggest collective learning. But the clues cannot tell us what words people used or who made the first tool.

speak.partnerTask: Tell your partner which clue gives the best evidence of shared learning, and why. Your partner names one thing that clue cannot prove. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud: "My claim is ... One clue is ... This matters because ..."

watch.title: Threshold 6: Humans and Collective Learning | Big History Project
watch.why: It explains collective learning, the main idea of this lesson, with short animations.
watch.beforeQuestion: Listen for the meaning of collective learning. What words does the video use?
watch.afterQuestion: Give one example of knowledge becoming more useful as people share it.
watch.summary: This video explains collective learning. Humans can use language to share ideas in great detail. So one person does not have to learn everything alone. Each generation can learn what older people knew and then add new ideas. Over time, knowledge grows. Early humans shared ways to find food, make tools, use fire and build shelter. This helped groups adapt to many different places, from hot lands to cold ones. We cannot hear what early people said. But tools slowly got better over time. This is a clue that people learned from each other. Collective learning did not make every group the same. Each community used what it knew in its own way, to fit its own place.
keyPoints: Humans share and build on knowledge across generations.
Archaeologists use clues like tools and hearths to study early learning.
Shared knowledge helped people adapt to many different places.

visual.description: A simple world map with Africa shaded as the place where our species first lived. Several soft, overlapping, faded arrows (not single lines) show groups spreading slowly into Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas, with the note 'over many thousands of years'. Small icons mark: a piece of engraved red ochre at Blombos Cave (South Africa), a hand stencil on a cave wall on Muna Island, near Sulawesi (Indonesia), and a small boat crossing the sea towards Australia. No exact dates on the arrows.
visual.alt: A world map showing early humans spreading slowly from Africa into Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas over many thousands of years.

sources.label: Smithsonian Human Origins: Blombos ocher plaque
Nature: Rock art from at least 67,800 years ago in Sulawesi

educatorNotes: Present the spread of early humans as a slow scientific process that took many thousands of years. Keep it separate from any modern movement of people, and do not ask learners to link it to their own lives.

The video may give an older date for the first Homo sapiens (about 200,000 years ago). Newer finds push this back to about 300,000 years ago. You can use this to show that science changes when new evidence is found.
Avoid calling early people 'primitive'. Their tools took planning, skill and teaching.
If you want a local example for the map, a hand stencil in a cave on Muna Island, near Sulawesi in Indonesia, is at least 67,800 years old (reported in Nature). It fits Clue 3.
